summary.text: For \(n\ge 20\), set \(d=D(n)\), \(e=D(d)\), and \(M=(n-e)/9\); padding \(d-1\) to \(M\) digits and adjoining its digitwise 9-complement and the digits of \(d\) produces \(q=d(10^M(10^M+1)-1)\) with \(D(q)=9M+e=n\), so \(k=10^nq>n\) satisfies \(d\mid k\) and \(D(k)=n\mid n\). The cases \(1\le n<20\) are handled by explicit partners.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(x)\) denote the sum of the ordinary base-ten digits of the nonnegative integer \(x\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive integer \(k\ne n\) such that
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
This says precisely that the set of Harshad amicable partners used to define \(a(n)\) is nonempty. Since every member of that set is positive, its least member is then positive, and hence \(a(n)\ne0\).

We first give the construction for \(n\ge20\).

Put
\[
d=D(n),\qquad e=D(d).
\]
Because \(n>0\), its leading decimal digit is nonzero, so \(d>0\).

We need two elementary estimates. If
\[
n=10t+r,\qquad 0\le r<10,
\]
then \(t=\lfloor n/10\rfloor\), and deleting the last decimal digit gives
\[
D(n)=r+D(t).
\]
For every nonnegative integer \(x\), one has \(D(x)\le x\): this follows immediately by induction from the same last-digit decomposition. Consequently
\[
d=D(n)=r+D(t)\le r+t,
\]
and likewise
\[
e=D(d)\le d.
\]
As \(n\ge20\), we have \(t\ge2\). Thus \(r\le9\le8t\), and hence
\[
2(r+t)\le r+10t=n.
\]
It follows that
\[
d+e\le2d\le2(r+t)\le n. \tag{1}
\]

We also use the standard congruence
\[
x\equiv D(x)\pmod 9. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, if \(x=\sum_i x_i10^i\) is its decimal expansion, then \(10^i\equiv1\pmod9\), so \(x\equiv\sum_i x_i=D(x)\pmod9\). Applying (2) first to \(n\) and then to \(d\) gives
\[
n\equiv d\equiv e\pmod9.
\]
By (1), \(e\le n\), so \(n-e\) is a nonnegative multiple of \(9\). Define
\[
M=\frac{n-e}{9}.
\]
Then
\[
9M=n-e. \tag{3}
\]
From (1),
\[
d\le n-e=9M. \tag{4}
\]
Since \(d>0\), (4) also shows that \(M>0\).

For every positive integer \(M\),
\[
9M<10^M. \tag{5}
\]
This can be seen by induction. For \(M=1\), it is \(9<10\). If \(9M<10^M\), then, since \(10^M\ge1\),
\[
9(M+1)=9M+9<10^M+9\le10^M+9\cdot10^M=10^{M+1}.
\]
Combining (4) and (5), and writing
\[
P=10^M,
\]
we obtain
\[
d\le9M<P. \tag{6}
\]
In particular, \(0\le d-1<P\), so \(d-1\) can be represented by exactly \(M\) decimal positions if leading zeroes are allowed.

Write those \(M\) digits, starting with the units digit, as
\[
A=(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{M-1}),
\]
where each \(0\le a_i\le9\) and
\[
d-1=\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}a_i10^i. \tag{7}
\]
Define the digitwise nine-complement block
\[
B=(9-a_0,9-a_1,\ldots,9-a_{M-1}),
\]
and let the integer represented by this block be
\[
c=\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}(9-a_i)10^i.
\]
There are two useful consequences of this complementing operation. First, the combined sum of the digits in \(A\) and \(B\) is
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}a_i+\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}(9-a_i)=9M. \tag{8}
\]
Second, by (7),
\[
\begin{aligned}
c+(d-1)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}\bigl((9-a_i)+a_i\bigr)10^i\\
&=9\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}10^i\\
&=10^M-1=P-1.
\end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]
Thus \(c=P-d\).

Now form a decimal integer \(q\) from three blocks, ordered from least significant to most significant as follows:

* the lowest \(M\) positions are the block \(B\);
* the next \(M\) positions are the block \(A\);
* above those are the ordinary decimal digits of \(d\).

Equivalently,
\[
q=c+P(d-1)+P^2d. \tag{10}
\]
All entries in these blocks are valid decimal digits. The top block is the ordinary expansion of the positive integer \(d\), so its leading digit is nonzero; therefore this concatenation is an ordinary decimal expansion of a positive integer.

The digit sum of \(q\) is now immediate from (8). The blocks \(A\) and \(B\) contribute \(9M\), while the final block, consisting of the digits of \(d\), contributes \(D(d)=e\). Hence, by (3),
\[
D(q)=9M+e=n. \tag{11}
\]

The same block construction also makes \(q\) divisible by \(d\). From (9), \(c=P-d\), and substituting this into (10) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
q
&=(P-d)+P(d-1)+P^2d\\
&=P-d+Pd-P+P^2d\\
&=d(P^2+P-1)\\
&=d\bigl(P(P+1)-1\bigr).
\end{aligned} \tag{12}
\]
Thus
\[
d=D(n)\mid q. \tag{13}
\]

Finally, define
\[
k=10^nq.
\]
Multiplication by \(10^n\) appends \(n\) zeroes to the decimal expansion of the positive integer \(q\), so it does not change the digit sum. Therefore (11) gives
\[
D(k)=D(q)=n,
\]
and in particular
\[
D(k)\mid n. \tag{14}
\]
Also, (13) implies
\[
D(n)=d\mid k. \tag{15}
\]
The integer \(k\) is positive. Moreover, since \(q\ge1\),
\[
k=10^nq\ge10^n>n.
\]
The last inequality holds for every positive \(n\), for example by the elementary induction \(10^n>n\). Hence \(k\ne n\). Equations (14) and (15) show that this \(k\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\). This proves existence for every \(n\ge20\).

It remains to handle \(1\le n\le19\). The following table gives an explicit partner \(k\) in each case. It also displays both digit sums, so all required divisibilities can be read off directly.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 n&D(n)&k&D(k)\\ \hline
 1&1&10&1\\
 2&2&10&1\\
 3&3&12&3\\
 4&4&20&2\\
 5&5&10&1\\
 6&6&12&3\\
 7&7&70&7\\
 8&8&40&4\\
 9&9&18&9\\
 10&1&1&1\\
 11&2&10&1\\
 12&3&3&3\\
 13&4&76&13\\
 14&5&10&1\\
 15&6&12&3\\
 16&7&35&8\\
 17&8&296&17\\
 18&9&9&9\\
 19&10&10&1
\end{array}
\]
For completeness, in every row \(k>0\) and \(k\ne n\). Also \(D(n)\mid k\): the only less visually immediate instances are \(7\mid35\), \(8\mid296\), and \(10\mid10\), which are clear. Finally \(D(k)\mid n\): in particular, for the special rows one has \(8\mid16\), \(17\mid17\), and \(13\mid13\); all other rows are equally immediate from the table. Thus every positive integer below \(20\) also has a partner.

We have therefore proved that for every positive integer \(n\), the set
\[
S_n=\{k\in\mathbb N: k>0,\ k\ne n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, \(S_n\) has a least element. By definition, \(a(n)\) is this least element when \(S_n\) is nonempty, and is \(0\) only when \(S_n\) is empty. Every element of \(S_n\), including its least element, is positive. Consequently
\[
a(n)>0,
\]
and hence \(a(n)\ne0\) for every positive integer \(n\), as required.
